KEY MESSAGE 1...Severe thunderstorms expected this afternoon through
this evening across portions of the area. 

Shower and thunderstorms are beginning to develop over the
higher terrain and in the lee of the Blue Ridge as of 2 PM EDT.
Not seeing much of anything developing on the Bay/River breezes,
so seems like the main threat will be with storms along the
lee trough and leading edge of the incoming shortwave this
afternoon/evening. Mostly sunny to partly cloudy skies
throughout the day have lead to MLCAPE values on the order of
1500-3000 J/kg with lowest amounts SW and higher amounts towards
the Chesapeake Bay into northeast MD. DCAPE values range from
500-800 J/kg, which is sufficient to produce some damaging wind
gusts with the strongest storms. The highest shear is along the
MD/PA border, with values around 20-25 knots. As a result of all
of this, a Severe Thunderstorm Watch was issued from areas
along/east of I-81 and north of US-50. Storms thus far have had
trouble really getting organized, which is likely due to weaker
lapse rates out west, and not quite having the strongest shear
we expect later in the afternoon. As storms move east, as well
as the subsequent outflows from said storms, expect them to grow
upscale and become stronger the closer we get to the I-95
corridor into northeast MD. This is where it seems like all of
the ingredients have the best chance of coming together for the
highest severe weather threat. That being said, any storms in
this environment could become severe and produce locally
damaging winds even outside of more organized clusters. Frequent
cloud-to-ground lightning can be expected with storms today, 
likely well ahead of and behind storms. Use extreme caution if 
outdoors later this afternoon and remember that when thunder 
roars to head indoors!

The severe threat should wane into the evening as we lose 
daytime heating. However, storms today will produce very heavy 
rainfall rates, perhaps as high as 3-4 inches/hour for short 
periods. Should this find the wrong area, and/or if an area sees
a couple back-to-back, a flash flooding threat isn't out of the
question. This threat is highest in northeast MD, which is 
where the best chance for colliding outflow boundaries and/or 
Bay Breeze interactions is. This could cause some localized 
training effects, which brought a few areas a quick 3 to 4 
inches yesterday, so can't completely rule that out. WPC has 
this area in a SLGT risk excessive rainfall outlook as a result.



KEY MESSAGE 2... Patchy morning fog, high humidity, hot 
temperatures, and daily thunderstorm chances continue through early 
next week. 

Somewhat similar conditions are expected Saturday as another 
potent shortwave passes through. The main difference is that
mid-level flow turns a bit more W to WSW versus the SW'ly flow
we have had in recent days. As a result, coverage of storms is
likely to be less than what we see today. However, shear values
increase a bit, reaching 30 to 35 kts as the subtropical jet 
stream begins to strengthen. Mid-level lapse rates are also
impressive, similar to today's event. Instability will be a bit
less tomorrow, owing to the westerly mid-level flow. 
Thermodynamic profiles depict skinnier CAPE profiles, but 
inverted-V signatures towards the surface. Our thoughts are 
that the coverage should be less tomorrow, but the ceiling could
be higher in terms of damaging wind potential, should storms be
able to develop and get organized. The Storm Prediction Center
has added a Marginal Risk for severe weather tomorrow as a
result that encompasses much of the forecast area, further
reinforcing our thoughts. 

Convection begins to wane a bit Sunday into Monday given quasi-zonal 
flow aloft. A few storms may develop over the higher elevations,
but coverage will be much less than in recent days. This will 
be short-lived however, with storm chances increasing once 
again Tuesday through the end of the week as a series of 
shortwave disturbances passing through. 

Outside of the storm chances expect highs in the upper 80s and low 
90s with heat indices east of the BLue Ridge up around 100 degrees. 
The hottest days look to be Sunday through Tuesday given the 
strengthened subtropical ridge over the region.


KEY MESSAGE 3...A cold front could arrive late next week and 
into the weekend bringing relief from the heat and humidity. 

While this is very far out in the forecast period, there is some 
signal that a more potent frontal system could push through the 
region late in the week. The details are murky at this stage of the 
forecast, with timing very uncertain, as well as potential impacts. 
Deterministic and ensemble guidance is generally between 
Thursday/Friday right now, with improvement in the weather pattern 
possible into the upcoming weekend. Any decent frontal passage in 
the summertime should be watched closely for potential severe
